newsitem.title: CHINA: China's leaders seen ending secret seaside conclave.
newsitem.headline: China's leaders seen ending secret seaside conclave.

text.p: China's top leaders have started to furl their beach umbrellas and head back to the city after secret seaside sessions on how to underline the importance of the private sector in the world's biggest communist state.

For about a month the most powerful men who head China's ruling Communist Party have been gathered in secret conclaves at the northern beach resort of Beidaihe to set the finishing touches to the policy document and personnel changes they will endorse at an upcoming five-yearly party congress.

Signs emerged that those meetings may be drawing to a close with Premier Li Peng due to leave on Thursday for Singapore and Malaysia. Vice Premier Qian Qichen was already back in Beijing to meet Bill Richardson, chief U.S. delegate to the United Nations.
What was decided -- if anything -- remains a mystery.

However, clues have emerged in China's state-run media, which operates as the mouthpiece for whichever leader has control of the propaganda apparatus. At present, analysts say, it is almost certain that party chief and state president Jiang Zemin commands the airwaves and the printing presses.
Economic reform is a topic of front-page debate.

One thing appears certain. From under the shade of their beach umbrellas, China's leaders seem to have taken the cool-headed decision to promote private enterprise as the sole means to revive their sagging state sector.

A string of editorials and interviews have urged China to break out of the ideological straitjacket of state as master, to cease to debate the merits of "socialism" versus "capitalist" and just to get on with the business of making money.
"At the 15th congress, the party will throw its approval behind the existence of private enterprise," said one senior Chinese economist who declined to be identified.

"We're not going to see any specific policy initiatives at the congress, but it will say what needs to be said," he said. "They will make clear to doubters, to leftists, that private enterprise is acceptable and can exist alongside the state sector. That is a major ideological breakthrough for us."

No mention has been made of who will coordinate that reform, although Chinese sources say Vice-Premier and economic tsar Zhu Rongji, one of the seven-member all-powerful Politburo standing committee, has emerged from under his umbrella as front-runner for the job of premier when it falls vacant next March.
Another official seen likely to win promotion at the party congress, due in September or October, is a woman, Foreign Trade Minister Wu Yi, who is in the running for a Politburo seat.
Jiang's closest aide, Zeng Qinghong, who currently heads the general office of the party central committee, is also expected to enter the Politburo.

Names bandied about as contenders for a coveted standing committee position include propaganda tsar Ding Guangen and General Zhang Wannian, vice chairman of the Central Military Commission, who would ensure an army presence at the top.

Rumour abounds. The latest is the revival at the beach of a proposal by Jiang to reinstate the posts of party chairman and vice-chairman -- thus enabling him to solve the vexing problem of finding a job for Premier Li when he steps down next March.
Li would be vice-chairman goes the rumour, similar to one that swirled and disappeared several months ago. Who knows?

Even in a China transformed by market reform, reading the tea-leaves -- and watching how long the television cameras linger on each official -- remain a means as reliable as any other to fathom the secretive internal workings of the party, diplomats say.
